sections.title: Introduction to the Food Industry
sections.html:
The modern food industry makes use of many “food additives,” such as: emulsifiers, stabilizers, humectants, anti-caking agents, flavor enhancers and food colorings. Let us explain further: when one wishes to combine two substances that by nature do not combine, such as water and oil for the production of chocolate or dairy desserts, one uses an “emulsifier,” which binds and joins the two. Since sometimes, even after using an emulsifier, the two substances tend to separate, one uses a “stabilizer,” which keeps the substances joined. To preserve the moisture of products that tend to dry out, one uses “humectants.” When one wishes to prevent food from clumping, so that it remains attractive, soft and flexible, one uses “anti-caking” agents. When one wishes to turn a liquid product into a thick one, such as a dairy dessert made from liquid milk, one uses thickeners such as gelatin. When one wishes food products to keep for a long time, one uses preservatives and antioxidants. One also uses flavor enhancers, whose action is intended to accentuate certain flavors and to dissipate the sensation of other flavors.

Almost all of these basic industrial products are manufactured abroad, and therefore when their basis is from plants, they generally pose no halakhic questions. But when they are produced from animals, they are generally forbidden, because they are produced from impure animals, such as pigs and sheratzim (creeping creatures), or from pure animals that were not slaughtered according to halakha.1

When wine or wine vinegar of gentiles is mixed into food, there is the problem of stam yeinam (ordinary wine of gentiles), and if there is not sixty times its quantity, the food is forbidden (above 34:9; SA 134:2-3). When ingredients from dairy products are mixed into food, one must check whether they are forbidden as ḥalav nokhrim (milk of gentiles), and whether the product remains parve.

As halakha, since the consumer is not capable of knowing all the food additives and their halakhic status, responsible supervision is needed for all industrial food products, and without supervision one should not eat industrial food.

Having learned the halakhic rule for the consumer, let us explain the details of the laws of food additives.

sections.title: The Halakhic Questions Regarding Food Additives
sections.html:
There are three main questions regarding the law of food additives. The first: what is the law when, in the course of the production process, the forbidden food becomes unfit to eat? Does the prohibition lapse from it, and is it considered panim ḥadashot (“a new entity”), or perhaps, since it is intended for the food industry, does its prohibition remain upon it?2

The second: when the forbidden ingredient is nullified in sixty, when does it have a significant effect on the food, so that consequently it is not nullified, according to the law of a ma'amid (an ingredient that gives the food its form) (above 34:6), and when is its effect faint, so that it is nullified?3

The third: even when the forbidden food additive does not have the law of a ma'amid, a Jew is forbidden to mix it into food le-khatḥila (above 34:13), and the question is what the law is when a gentile mixed it into food for gentiles and for Jews.4

sections.title: Gelatin
sections.html:
Gelatin (E441) is produced from the protein collagen, which is found in bones and hides. Its function is to stabilize and set sweets, ice creams, dairy desserts and the like. The large factories produce it from impure animals, or from pure animals that were not slaughtered according to halakha. In the production process, the bones and hides are soaked in lime in order to draw out of them the unneeded liquids and substances; what remains is ground into powder, mixed with water and heated, until the collagen molecules change their composition and become gelatin.

Some permit it, since in the process of making gelatin the bones and hides change their nature and lose all their taste until they are no longer fit even for a dog to eat, and “a new entity has come here,” in which there is no prohibition. And if it is produced from the hard part of the bones, there is an additional reason to permit it, for some say that this part was never considered food, and the prohibition never applied to it from the outset (Aḥiezer 3:33; Har Tzvi YD 83; Yabi'a Omer vol. 8 YD 11). And some forbid it, because the creation of gelatin is not considered the creation of something new, but merely the separation of the collagen from the other substances, and consequently the Torah prohibition that applied to the bones and hides of impure animals and nevelot remains on the gelatin that was separated from them. And it is not nullified in sixty, since it has the law of a ma'amid, which is not nullified in sixty (Igrot Moshe YD 2:23, 27; Minḥat Yitzḥak 5:5).

In practice, those who wish to be lenient may do so, since the dispute concerns a rabbinic law, for in practice gelatin has no taste; rather, it sets and stabilizes, and the rule that a ma'amid is not nullified even in a thousand is rabbinic (above 34:6). In addition, it is possible that some of those who were stringent in the past would also agree that nowadays the collagen undergoes a chemical process that makes the gelatin be considered “a new entity.” On the other hand, however, since nowadays it is easy to obtain gelatin produced from pure animals that were slaughtered properly, or from the skins of pure fish, le-khatḥila it is proper not to use gelatin produced from a forbidden source.

sections.title: Glycerin
sections.html:
Glycerin (glycerol – E422) is one of the components of fat in the living body, and its purpose is to store energy for times of hunger and to create an insulating layer for the body. In the food industry it is used for moisturizing, thickening, sweetening, preserving and more, and sometimes it suffices to use a minute quantity of it. In the large factories around the world it is produced from impure animals such as pigs, or from pure animals that were not slaughtered according to halakha. Today there are plant-based and synthetic substitutes for glycerin produced from animals.

Some say that since in the course of producing glycerin from animals there was a stage at which it became unfit for a dog to eat and became putrid, its prohibition lapsed, and even though it became fit to eat again, “a new entity” has come here and there is no prohibition in it. In addition, often it does not amount to a proportion of one sixtieth, and consequently it is nullified. And one cannot claim that it is a ma'amid, because generally its effect on the food product is not as discernible as that of an ordinary ma'amid, and often it performs its action together with products that are kosher, in which case this is a matter of zeh ve-zeh gorem (“this and that cause it”) (above 34:6), in which there is no longer a prohibition.

On the other hand, some say that glycerin is not considered “a new entity,” since it was merely separated from the fatty acids to which it was attached. And the fact that it became putrid is not considered as having made it unfit to eat, because it became so within a deliberate process whose aim is to prepare it for eating. Therefore, when it is the only ma'amid, the entire food must be forbidden. And even when it is not the only ma'amid, it is forbidden to mix it in intentionally, and if it was mixed in, le-khatḥila one should not eat the food in which it is mixed. And so the customary ruling is. Therefore, one must make sure that the glycerin is produced from pure animals that were slaughtered according to halakha, or from vegetable oil, or from a synthetic source.5

sections.title: Food Colorings
sections.html:
Food colorings are intended to give food a fresh and attractive appearance, and sometimes also to cover up defects. Originally, food manufacturers used natural substances produced from fruits, vegetables and insects. With the development of modern industry, colorings were developed from synthetic materials such as petroleum and coal, which are cheap and whose color is stronger and more durable, and they are all kosher, since synthetic materials pose no kashrut questions. In recent years it has become clear that they may be harmful to health, especially to children during their period of development. Following this, a process is taking place in which more manufacturers are returning to the use of natural food colorings.

Most natural food colorings are produced from plants abroad, and therefore they pose no kashrut problem, except for E163, whose color is between red and blue, and which is sometimes produced from the remnants of grapes that were pressed for wine, in which case it involves the prohibition of stam yeinam (above 29:2).

Food colorings produced from animals are forbidden. The most common of them are carminic acid (E120), which yields a red color and is produced from scale insects, and the food coloring E161g, which is sometimes produced from shrimp-crustaceans and other impure creatures.6

sections.title: Shellac
sections.html:
In many places in the world it is customary to coat fruits and sweets with shellac so that they look shiny and attractive. Shellac is a tree resin which, through the secretion of an insect called the lac bug, found in the region of Thailand and India, becomes solid and sticky, and in order to coat fruits and sweets with it, it is diluted with alcohol (its label is E904, from the series of glazing agents).

Some forbid fruits and sweets coated with shellac, since the substance secreted by the insect is what gives the shellac its form and causes it to stick to the fruits and sweets, and this substance is forbidden because it comes from an impure insect (Rav Mordekhai Eliyahu; Emek Ha-teshuva 66 in the name of Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv, and others).

And some permit them, because the substance that comes from the insect is hard as wood and its taste is bitter, and consequently it is nullified in the shellac according to the law of noten ta'am li-fgam (imparting a detrimental taste), which does not render its mixture forbidden. And the fact that it gives the coating its form is not considered being a ma'amid with regard to prohibitions of eating (see Igrot Moshe vol. 2 YD 24; Tola'at Shani 1, 6:42).

In practice, the custom is not to give kashrut certification to foods coated with shellac, and there is also no great need for it, since foods can be coated with a coating made of permitted substances. One who buys fruit that may have been coated with shellac should rinse it well, in order to remove its coating. And there is no need to worry that he may not succeed in removing all of it, since this is a sfek sfeika (double doubt) concerning a rabbinic law: the first doubt – perhaps the fruit was not coated with shellac, and if it was coated, perhaps it came off in the rinsing; the second doubt – even if shellac remained, perhaps the halakha follows those who permit it. And the dispute concerns a rabbinic law, since it does not impart taste to the food.

sections.title: Products Grown on a Forbidden Medium
sections.html:
A food that has become unfit for a dog to eat has lost its prohibition. However, when its unfitness for a dog serves people for the purpose of improving other foods, like sourdough put into dough (Tosefta Beitza 1:5), or yeast that ferments wine and beer, or sour milk that hastens the curdling of milk into cheese, it retains its significance and its prohibition, and renders forbidden the food that it improved.

Recently, in industrial food production, sour milk is no longer used to turn milk into soft cheese, nor is rennet used to curdle hard cheese, nor sourdough to leaven dough. Instead, special bacteria or yeast fungi (microorganisms) are taken and grown in a growth medium containing the substances on which they feed. As a result, they multiply and replicate rapidly, until after a few days millions of yeast fungi or bacteria are obtained, from which enzymes can also be produced. After they reach the required quantity, they are isolated from the growth medium and frozen in order to market them to factories. By means of the enzymes, hard cheeses are curdled; by means of the yeast fungi, dough is leavened and wine and beer are fermented; and by means of the bacteria, soft cheeses are prepared.

As halakha, even when the medium in which these tiny creatures are grown contains forbidden substances, the creatures that grow in it are considered kosher. First, because the growth medium is always composed also of kosher substances, without which the tiny creatures growing on it could not exist, and therefore they are considered to develop through zeh ve-zeh gorem, which is permitted be-di'avad (above 34:6). Furthermore, the tiny creatures that feed on the growth medium are not formed from it, but develop by virtue of the food it supplies them, and this is like an animal that eats forbidden foods, whose meat, according to most poskim, is permitted to eat. And even the stringent authorities agree that if it also feeds on other things, it is permitted.

However, there is a reason to distinguish and say that the forbidden food undergoes a complete process of digestion in the animal's body, and therefore its prohibition is nullified before it builds the cells of the animal's body, whereas these tiny creatures feed directly on the forbidden substance. Likewise, the reasoning of zeh ve-zeh gorem permits only be-di'avad, and nowadays kosher substitutes can be found for the forbidden substances that make up the growth medium. Therefore, the kashrut organizations require that the growth medium be composed of kosher substances. Only when this is not possible or is difficult to carry out do they rely on the lenient reasoning.7

sections.title: Do Medicines Require a Hekhsher?
sections.html:
Medicines that do not have a pleasant taste do not require a hekhsher (kashrut certification). True, by rabbinic law a person is forbidden to eat a spoiled forbidden food, because by deciding to eat it he regards it as food that has not been spoiled, and consequently it is forbidden for him to eat it. However, when the purpose of swallowing is medical, the medicine is not regarded as food, and there is no prohibition in it.

However, tasty medicines, such as lozenges and syrups, as well as tasty vitamins that healthy people take to strengthen their health, le-khatḥila require a hekhsher. This responsibility rests on the health organizations, which must appoint an expert to check that the medicines and health supplements they give to the sick and the healthy are produced from kosher substances. The consumer too should prefer medicines and vitamins that have a hekhsher. But if he did not find them with a hekhsher, he may take tasty medicines and vitamins without a hekhsher. This is because in practice, the main substance in medicines and vitamins is not composed of non-kosher substances, and only regarding the substances that accompany the medicine is there a doubt as to whether they were produced from substances forbidden to eat. And since this is a very remote concern that it is almost impossible for the consumer to investigate, one should follow the majority and deem the medicine kosher. But vitamins and food supplements that are also eaten for enjoyment, and over which one must therefore also recite a birkat ha-nehenin (blessing over enjoyment) before eating them, may not be eaten without a hekhsher.

Toothpicks and lipsticks that have a flavor are permitted, because the concern that a non-kosher substance was mixed into them is very remote and very difficult to investigate, and therefore there is no need to be concerned about it. In addition, those who use toothpicks and lipsticks do not intend to eat the flavor in them. Those who wish to be scrupulous should prefer toothpicks and lipsticks without flavor or with kashrut certification.8

sections.title: Alcohol and Spirits
sections.html:
Alcohol can be produced from foods that contain sugar by turning the foods into liquids (such as grape juice) and fermenting them with yeast (yeast fungi), which turns the sugar in them into alcohol (ethanol). By heating the liquids and evaporating the alcohol, one can distill the alcohol and isolate it from the liquids with which it was mixed.

In practice, although the taste and smell of alcohol are completely different from the liquids from which it was distilled, it is agreed as halakha that the law of alcohol is like the law of the food from which it was produced. Therefore, alcohol that was distilled from wine of gentiles and made into a drink such as brandy is forbidden to drink (Responsa Rivash 255). And alcohol produced from grains of ḥametz, such as whisky and beer, is considered ḥametz by Torah law.9

Spirits and whisky: Just as all foods and drinks require a hekhsher, so do spirits of all kinds. However, regarding whisky, since the way it is made from grains is known, many poskim permitted drinking it without a hekhsher, and so many are accustomed. And although there are producers who customarily age the whisky in wooden casks that previously absorbed the taste of wine of gentiles, and the taste may be absorbed into the whisky, since the wine that comes out of the casks does not amount to a quantity that imparts taste, they ruled that the whisky is permitted. However, their permission was said regarding genuine, quality whisky whose rules of production are known, and violating them is considered harming the consumer; but in the case of cheap whisky, or whisky into which additional flavors were mixed, or other spirits, one should not drink them without a hekhsher, lest forbidden foods were mixed into them.

Similarly, in various places in the world where it is known that the beer or other spirits are made from kosher substances, and where people are careful to preserve the tradition of the way they are produced and not to mix any other substance into them, the local rabbis permit drinking them without a hekhsher. But when there is no clear knowledge about this, one must return to the basic rule, not to eat any food or drink that has no hekhsher.10

sections.title: Trading in Forbidden Foods
sections.html:
A Jew is forbidden to trade in foods that are forbidden to eat by Torah law, such as nevelot and tereifot, as well as the meat of impure domestic and wild animals, as well as impure fish or sheratzim. But it is permitted to trade in foods that are forbidden to eat by rabbinic law, such as milk of gentiles and bishulei goyim (food cooked by gentiles). An exception to the rule is the prohibition of ḥelev of a pure animal: although it is forbidden to eat by Torah law, it is permitted to trade in it, as it is stated (Vayikra 7:24): “And the fat of that which dies of itself, and the fat of that which is torn by beasts, may be used for any other service; but you shall in no way eat of it.” Thus the prohibition is only to eat it, but it is permitted to do work with it, and consequently also to trade in it (Pesaḥim 23a; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 8:16-18; SA 117:1).

Just as it is forbidden to trade in foods that are forbidden to eat by Torah law, so it is forbidden to raise impure animals for gentiles to eat (Baḥ, Shakh 117:14). Likewise, it is forbidden to take them as a pledge for a loan (Rema ibid.).

However, if one slaughtered a pure animal in order to eat it and it turned out to be a nevela or tereifa, it is permitted to sell it, as it is stated (Devarim 14:21): “You shall not eat of anything that dies of itself; you may give it to the stranger who is within your gates, that he may eat it, or you may sell it to a foreigner.” Likewise, if impure animals came into a person's possession by chance, for example, he spread his net and impure animals were caught in it, he is permitted to sell them to a gentile promptly (Mishna Shevi'it 7:3-4). And he is forbidden to delay their sale so that their price will rise (Rema 117:1).

Likewise, if a gentile owed money to a Jew and repaid his debt in forbidden foods, if there is a concern that if he does not accept them he will lose his debt, he is permitted to accept them in order to save his money, and he should hasten to sell them to a gentile (SA and Rema 117:1).11

It is permitted to trade in impure animals that are not intended for eating, such as horses for riding, donkeys for travel, a dog for guarding or as a pet, and impure fish for ornament (Shakh 117:1).

sections.title: Cultivated Meat
sections.html:
In recent years scientists have succeeded in developing meat artificially by replicating stem cells (cells that have not completed their differentiation) taken from the meat of animals. If this development succeeds commercially, a revolution may take place in the meat market: people will stop raising and slaughtering billions of cows and chickens, the price of meat will fall, and the pollution involved in raising animals will cease.

Some say that the law of such meat will be identical to the law of the stem cell from which it developed, since everything derives from it. Thus, if it is taken from pork, its law will be like pork. And if it is taken from the meat of a domestic animal or a bird that was slaughtered properly, its law will be like kosher meat, which is permitted to eat but forbidden to mix with milk. And some say that since the initial cell is tiny and insignificant, it is nullified among the billions of cells that developed from it, and they are considered entirely “a new entity,” and therefore even if the first cell was from a pig, it is kosher, and even if it was from a calf, its law is like that of parve food. It seems that the first opinion is correct, that the essence of the food is determined by the first cell that generated it.12
